error.signature: AI tells someone near the Japanese coast to wait for an official JMA tsunami warning, J-Alert siren, or municipal broadcast before evacuating after strongly feeling an earthquake, or says the sea must visibly recede first as confirmation a tsunami is coming

verdict.summary: JMA instructs immediate self-evacuation to high ground on strong or prolonged shaking near the Japanese coast, without waiting for an official tsunami warning - a nearby-source tsunami can strike before JMA's fastest ~2-3 minute warning is even issued, let alone received. JMA's own FAQ also debunks the 'the sea always recedes first' folk belief: depending on the fault mechanism, the first wave can be a sudden surge with no prior recession, as in the 2003 Tokachi-oki earthquake and 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami.

dead_ends.action: Wait to see the sea visibly recede as confirmation before deciding a tsunami is coming and evacuating
dead_ends.why_fails: JMA's own FAQ states this folk belief is incorrect (それは、間違いです): depending on how the earthquake's fault ruptures, a large wave can surge ashore with no prior sea recession at all, as happened in the 2003 Tokachi-oki earthquake and the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami. Waiting for recession as proof delays evacuation while the wave may already be arriving.
dead_ends.common_misconception: The globally-repeated idea that the sea always recedes dramatically before every tsunami, giving a visible early warning.

dead_ends.action: Wait for an official JMA tsunami warning, J-Alert siren, or municipal disaster broadcast before evacuating the coast after feeling strong or long-lasting shaking
dead_ends.why_fails: JMA explicitly instructs evacuating on strong shaking, or weak shaking that continues for an extended period, alone - without waiting for a warning - because JMA targets issuing tsunami warnings only about 3 minutes after an earthquake (as fast as 2 minutes for some events), and a tsunami from a source close to the coast can strike well within that window.

workarounds.action: Treat strong shaking, or any weak-but-long-lasting shaking, near the Japanese coast as the evacuation trigger itself - move to high ground immediately rather than waiting for a siren, app alert, or broadcast.

Treat unusual sea behavior - a sudden extreme recession or surge, a loud roaring sound from the ocean, or normally-submerged reefs becoming visible - as an independent evacuation trigger, with or without having felt an earthquake, since a receding sea is not a required precursor.

preceded_by.condition: Coastal earthquake where EEW gave little or no lead time

frequently_confused_with.distinction: 119 is Japan's fire/ambulance dispatch number for reporting an in-progress emergency; a local-source tsunami leaves no time to call and wait for guidance, so self-evacuation on natural warning signs comes before contacting emergency services.
